passage:
Sit, Gurleen. Your Tarun Mama knows this feeling better than you think. When I was twenty, my scholarship letter was late. My closest friend at college worked part-time in the office, and he saw a notice that the scholarship had been cut. He said nothing for a month. In that month I turned down a tutoring job, because I thought the money was coming.
When I found out, from the notice board, I went cold. He said, "I didn't want to be the one to hurt you." But he hadn't saved me from anything. He had only taken away my chance to choose. It hurt as much as if he had lied to my face. We did make up, years later, but it took a long time.

qa.q: Where did Tarun find out the scholarship had been cut?
qa.a: Tarun found out from the notice board.

qa.q: Why did the friend's silence hurt Tarun as much as a lie?
qa.a: Tarun had turned down a tutoring job believing the money was coming, so he felt his chance to choose had been taken away.

qa.q: What choice by the friend turned out badly, and what would have been better?
qa.a: The friend chose silence to avoid hurting Tarun; telling him straight away would have let him keep the tutoring job and decide for himself.

qa.q: How might the friend have felt while keeping the notice to himself for a month?
qa.a: He probably felt uneasy and afraid of bringing bad news, which is why he said, "I didn't want to be the one to hurt you."

grounding: An uncle recalls discovering that a close friend knew his scholarship was cut and stayed silent, which hurt like a direct lie because it took away his choice.

passage:
The power had been out for an hour, and rain hammered the window, when Vasudha got the message from their third flatmate: "Sorry for the short notice! Keerthana's known for weeks, I thought she'd have told you. I move out on Sunday."
Weeks. In those weeks Vasudha had turned down a cheaper room near her college, because here the rent was split three ways.
Keerthana came in with two lit candles. Vasudha held up the phone, its light bright in the dark. "You knew." Keerthana's face fell. "It wasn't my news to tell." "Maybe not," Vasudha said, her voice shaking, "but you watched me say no to that room." They sat without speaking, the rain still loud, the candles dripping onto a steel plate.

qa.q: What was the weather like when Vasudha got the message?
qa.a: Rain hammered the window, and the power had been out for an hour.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she said, "You knew"?
qa.a: She felt hurt and betrayed; her voice was shaking because Keerthana's silence had cost her the chance to take a cheaper room.

qa.q: What could Keerthana have done instead of staying silent?
qa.a: She could have urged the third flatmate to tell Vasudha soon, or warned Vasudha herself, since the news changed Vasudha's decision about the room.

qa.q: Why might Keerthana have believed she was doing the right thing?
qa.a: She thought it wasn't her news to tell and may have felt bound to the third flatmate, not trying to hurt Vasudha.

grounding: On a stormy night a young woman learns her flatmate knew important news and stayed silent, and the hurt feels as sharp as a lie because she lost the chance to decide.

passage:
The placement cell office was loud with the usual end-of-term chaos when Uday walked in holding his signed offer letter from the startup.
Aparna, his closest friend since first year, was at the front desk as a student volunteer. She looked at the letter and her face changed.
"You signed?"
"This morning. Why?"
She was quiet too long. Then: "My cousin works there. They haven't paid salaries for three months."
Uday stared at her. "Since when do you know?"
"Since… Diwali."
"Diwali. Aparna, I told you about this interview in October. You helped me prepare."
"I didn't want to crush your excitement. It's not my business."
Uday put the letter down. He felt stupid, and then angry, and then just very tired. It wasn't that she had lied. She hadn't said anything at all. And that silence had made the choice for him.

qa.q: How long have salaries not been paid at the startup?
qa.a: They haven't paid salaries for three months.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when Aparna said "Since Diwali"?
qa.a: He felt stupid, then angry, and then very tired, hurt that his closest friend stayed silent about something that changed his decision.

qa.q: What could Uday do now?
qa.a: He could speak to the placement cell staff about what he just learned and check his options before joining, rather than decide alone in anger.

qa.q: Why might Aparna have stayed silent?
qa.a: Aparna says she didn't want to crush Uday's excitement and felt it wasn't her business, though her silence took away his chance to decide with full information.

grounding: It shows a young adult discovering that a friend knew important information and stayed silent, and feeling the hurt of a denied choice.

passage:
Dear Nirmala,
I'm writing this because I can't say it without crying, and I don't want to cry at you.
Today Sir told me he gave the lead role in the dance competition to someone else. He said he decided three weeks ago. Three weeks, Nirmala. You were in that meeting. You knew.
Every night since then I've stayed back after practice. I skipped Amma's birthday dinner to rehearse. You watched me do the final spin forty times and said, "Looking good." You never said, "Preeti, stop, he's already decided."
I know you probably didn't want to be the one to break it to me. I know it wasn't your decision. But I would rather have been hurt three weeks ago than feel this stupid now. I could have chosen differently. I could have gone to Amma's dinner.
I still want us to be friends. I just need you to understand why this hurts.
Preeti

qa.q: When did Sir decide to give the lead role to someone else?
qa.a: He said he decided three weeks ago.

qa.q: What is Preeti feeling as she writes the letter?
qa.a: Preeti feels hurt and foolish, because Nirmala's silence let Preeti keep sacrificing time for a role that was already gone.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do to repair the friendship?
qa.a: Nirmala could apologise directly for staying silent and promise to share what affects Preeti's choices in future.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have seen her silence at the time?
qa.a: Nirmala may have thought the silence spared Preeti pain, not realising it took away Preeti's chance to decide with full information.

grounding: A young adult writes to a friend who knew important news and stayed silent, showing hurt as sharp as for a direct lie.

passage:
You know what the worst part is? It's not that Arnab took the job in Pune. I'm genuinely happy for him. It's that he applied in March. March. And we signed the lease on our Kolkata flat together in April.
I only found out on Sunday because his friend congratulated him at lunch, in front of me, about "the big move." I just sat there smiling like an idiot while everyone looked at me.
Later he said, "I didn't want to worry you till it was certain." But I'm Pema, I'm not a child. I plan things. If I'd known in March, maybe I'd have looked for work in Pune too. Maybe we'd have talked about long distance. Maybe we wouldn't have signed that lease.
He didn't lie. Not once. He just let me build my whole year on half the picture. And somehow that feels worse than a lie.

qa.q: When did Arnab apply for the job in Pune?
qa.a: He applied in March.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling while sitting at the lunch?
qa.a: Pema felt humiliated and blindsided, forced to smile while learning in front of others about a move Arnab had kept silent about.

qa.q: What would you advise Pema to do next?
qa.a: Pema could tell Arnab calmly that silence about big decisions hurts as much as lying, and agree together to share plans that affect both of them early.

qa.q: Why might Arnab have kept the application quiet?
qa.a: He says he did not want Pema to worry until it was certain, but his silence kept Pema from making Pema's own choices about the lease and her work.

grounding: It shows a young adult discovering a partner stayed silent about a major plan, and why that hurts like a lie by denying a fair choice.

passage:
Monday: Deepak signed the lease for the flat near college. The landlord was his friend Bhavna's cousin. Bhavna came along and smiled through the whole thing.
Thursday: at the canteen, a neighbour mentioned the building was due for demolition in six months. Deepak laughed it off. Then he saw Bhavna go very still.
"You knew?"
"My cousin told me last month. I thought he'd tell you. I didn't want to get in the middle."
Deepak felt something drop in his chest. She hadn't lied. She had just watched him sign.
The following Sunday: he had arranged to break the lease, losing the deposit. When Bhavna called, he said, "It's not that you lied. You let me decide without the one thing that mattered. That hurts the same." She was quiet, then said, "You're right. I'm sorry." He believed her. He just needed some time.

qa.q: When was the building due for demolition?
qa.a: In six months.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when Bhavna went still?
qa.a: Deepak felt something drop in his chest, hurt and betrayed that she had watched him sign without a word.

qa.q: How did Deepak explain the hurt to Bhavna?
qa.a: He told her plainly that her silence took away his chance to decide with full information, and that it hurt as much as a lie.

qa.q: Why might Bhavna have stayed silent?
qa.a: Bhavna didn't want to get in the middle between Deepak and her cousin, and assumed the cousin would tell him.

grounding: Shows a young man discovering a friend knew something important and stayed silent, and feeling the hurt as sharply as a direct lie.
